title: Load the press, run the cycle with both hands on the run buttons, unload
instruction: Load the blue block into the press nest between the rails, then run the press cycle: hold both yellow run buttons down at the same time, one with each gripper, pressing them within half a second of each other and keeping both held for two seconds. Never have a gripper near the nest while a button is pressed. Then let go of the buttons and move the block into the grey tray.
context: A two-hand control device starts a hazardous machine cycle (a press, shear or bender) only while both run buttons are held at once: both hands are then on the buttons, so neither is in the die. ISO 13851 (two-hand control devices) and ANSI B11.19 (performance requirements for risk reduction measures) describe them: the buttons are spaced so one hand cannot reach both, the cycle starts only when both are actuated within a short time of each other (synchronous actuation, 0.5 s for the strictest type) and runs only while both stay held; a hand in the die while a button is pressed is the hazard the device exists to prevent. Press operators (O*NET 51-4031, Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic) do this cycle many hundreds of times a shift. Here the two run buttons stand at the far left and far right of the bench, each in reach of one arm only, so loading the part, running the cycle and unloading it needs both arms, and the hand discipline (no gripper near the die while any button is pressed; both pressed within 0.5 s; both held 2 s) is scored at every control step, not only at the end. The press is an unpowered bench mock-up: the ram is not modelled and nothing moves when the cycle runs.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Six kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Press nest (the die): four dark grey steel locating rails, each 8 mm thick and 8 mm tall, fixed to the table round a 36 x 36 mm floor (the table) centred at x 30.0 cm, y 0: two rails running along y, 52 mm long, centred at x 32.2 and 27.8 cm, and two running along x, 36 mm long, centred at y +2.2 and -2.2 cm; the rails' inner faces are at x 28.2 and 31.8 cm and y +-1.8 cm. (2) Press frame (the press body): a grey steel wall 10 mm along x, 160 mm along y and 120 mm tall, fixed to the table centred at x 36.5 cm, y 0 (its near face at x 36.0 cm, 34 mm behind the back rail). The ram is not in the scene. (3) Part: a loose blue anodised aluminium block, a 30 mm cube, 70 g, standing with its sides parallel to x and y on (4) the feed mark: a thin white rigid plastic plate, 40 x 40 mm and 2 mm thick, fixed to the table centred at x 24.0 cm, y +12.0 cm (in reach of both arms). (5) Two run buttons: yellow rigid cylinders, 40 mm in diameter and 20 mm tall, fixed to the table standing at x 20.0 cm, y +21.0 cm (the left button; the right arm reaches no further left than about y +17 cm here) and x 20.0 cm, y -21.0 cm (the right button; the left arm reaches no further right than about y -18 cm here); 42 cm apart, so no single gripper can be on both. (6) Output tray: a grey rigid plastic tray, four walls 6 mm thick and 15 mm tall round a floor 80 mm along x and 140 mm along y, fixed to the table centred at x 16.0 cm, y 0 (in reach of both arms); in simulation the table top is its floor. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole trial: every control step (20 Hz) it reads the part and, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's tool point, finger-tip point (between the tips) and opening (0 closed, 1 fully open with the fingers 94 mm apart). It cannot see a gripper's heading, so each gripper's 'finger zone' is every point within a radius of the segment from its finger-tip point to 38 mm back up the gripper, the radius reaching a finger's outer corner (half the current finger gap plus the 8 mm finger thickness, and half the fingers' 27 mm width across; 57 mm fully open, 21 mm closed). The 'die space' is x 25.0 to 35.0 cm, y -5.0 to +5.0 cm, from the table up to 20 cm above it; a gripper is 'in the die space' when any point of its finger zone is inside it. Each run button is scored by its own arm only (the left button by the left gripper, the right by the right). A button is 'pressed' when that gripper's finger-tip point is within 16 mm of the button's axis horizontally and between 5 mm below and 10 mm above the button's top (20 mm above the table), with its opening 0.5 or less (fingers at most 47 mm apart); it is 'released' when that point is more than 30 mm above the button's top or more than 30 mm from its axis. The part is 'seated' when its centre is within 4 mm of the nest's centre horizontally, its lowest point within 3 mm of the table top and it is tilted less than 5 degrees (the rails leave it 3 mm each way, so a flat part between them is always seated; one up on a rail is not). A 'double press' begins on the first step on which both buttons are pressed and lasts while both stay pressed on every step; it is 'synchronous' if the two presses began (the first step of each button's current unbroken pressed span) within 0.5 s (10 steps) of each other. A 'cycle' is a synchronous double press that lasts at least 2.0 s (40 steps) with the part seated on every one of those steps; once a cycle has completed the part is 'cycled' for the rest of the trial. A 'breach' is any control step on which a button is pressed while any gripper is in the die space. The part 'rests in the tray' when its centre is over the tray's 80 x 140 mm floor and its lowest point is within 3 mm of the table top. A gripper has 'let go' of the part when its opening is 0.9 or more (fingers at least 84.5 mm apart) or its finger zone is more than 10 mm from the part. Score 0 if there was a breach at any moment, whatever happens afterwards, or if the part ends off the table (lowest point more than 10 mm below the table top). Otherwise, at the last step: 1.0 if the part is cycled, rests in the tray, both buttons are released and both grippers have let go of it; 0.75 if the part is cycled but does not rest in the tray (still in the nest, held, on the table elsewhere, on a tray wall), or rests in the tray with a button still pressed (or neither pressed nor released) or a gripper still holding it; 0.5 if the part is seated in the nest and a double press began while it was seated but no cycle completed (not synchronous, held under 2 s, or the part unseated during it); 0.25 if the part is seated in the nest and no double press began with it seated; 0 in every other case (the part on the feed mark, beside the nest, up on a rail, in the tray uncycled: skipping the cycle earns nothing; both buttons pressed with the part not in the nest is an empty cycle and counts for nothing). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. The score is read at the last step: the trial ends early (success) once the 1.0 conditions have held with the part still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers cannot be read, no press is registered (a running double press is broken and must begin again), no breach is recorded, and 'released' and 'let go' are taken as met; such steps are counted in the trace. In a real trial the buttons are two real run buttons wired to a lamp each and a third lamp that lights only while both are closed, the die space's outline and its 20 cm top are marked on the bench and a side card, and the trial is judged frame by frame from top and side video at 20 frames a second: any frame with a lamp lit and a finger inside the die outline below the 20 cm mark is a breach; the two lamps lighting more than 10 frames apart is not synchronous; the third lamp lit for 40 consecutive frames with the part between the rails is a cycle; the part's place in the nest and the tray is checked with a rule against the rails and the tray walls.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction. The rails, frame, feed mark, buttons and tray are fixed; the part is a plain uniform cube of the stated size and mass. The press is unpowered: the ram is not modelled (nothing is above the nest, so the part is loaded and unloaded straight down) and nothing moves during the cycle. The run buttons are fixed cylinders with no travel: 'pressed' is scored from a gripper's finger-tip height and position over its button with the fingers closed, not from a switch. Only the fingers are watched (38 mm up from the tips, as a round zone wider than the real fingers across their closing direction), not the wrist or forearm; with top-down grasps the fingers are the first and lowest part of an arm to enter the die space. Each button is scored only by its own arm's gripper; the buttons stand 42 cm apart, out of the other arm's reach, so this changes nothing a real pair of hands could do.
reset_notes: Put the part back flat on the feed mark centred at x 24.0 cm, y +12.0 cm, sides parallel to x and y. Nothing is consumed.
